name: Swarms
description: Python framework for building single agents and multi-agent systems (sequential, concurrent, hierarchical, graph workflows) on LiteLLM.
scored_configuration: Python library defaults: Agent() constructor arguments (max_loops=1, telemetry on), with the first-class autonomous mode (max_loops='auto', selected_tools='all') scored for tool-path criteria.
headline: Swarms ships almost no safety controls on its tool path: no approval gate, no sandbox, no argument validation, and no restriction after reading untrusted content. Its autonomous mode gives the model a host shell with the full environment behind only a denylist that is not a strict boundary, plus file tools that accept any absolute path. Telemetry is on by default and sends tasks, outputs and agent configuration to a vendor endpoint, and secret handling and transport security are not locked down either.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: Swarms agents run with whatever authority the hosting Python process has. LLM provider keys come from environment variables (including any .env found above the working directory), and the autonomous mode's shell tool and every stdio MCP server inherit the full process environment. There is no per-tool identity, no scoped credential, and no authorization check anywhere on the tool path, so a hijacked agent acts with the operator's full local and cloud authority.

S.finding: No dedicated identity: the shell tool runs as the OS user with the inherited environment and the MCP stdio launcher copies all of os.environ.
S.gap: Use a dedicated, role-scoped identity instead of the operator's ambient credentials.

C.finding: No authorization layer exists; registered tools are called directly with model-supplied arguments.
C.gap: Route at least the main tool path through an authorization check in code.

evidence.note: All hits are docstrings or prompt text ('confirm completion', 'Confirmation message'); no approval gate exists on any tool path.

D.finding: Default install inherits all of the operator's environment and any .env credentials; narrowing requires the developer to build it.
D.gap: Ship a minimal default role and scrub the environment passed to tools.

B.finding: With bash on the host as the user and the full environment, a hijack reaches the user's entire account (SSH keys, cloud CLIs, tokens).
B.gap: Bound what the agent's credentials can reach to one system or project.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: There is no human approval step anywhere in the framework. The tool executor calls registered Python functions directly, the autonomous mode runs shell commands, writes and deletes files, and spawns sub-agents without asking anyone, and MCP tool calls go straight to the server. Interactive mode only asks the human for the next task, not for permission to act.

S.finding: No approval mechanism exists; tool calls go straight from model output to func(**arguments).
S.gap: Add per-call human approval showing the exact call for consequential tools.

evidence.note: All hits are docstrings or prompt text ('confirm completion', 'Confirmation message'); no approval gate exists on any tool path.

C.finding: The most powerful path (run_bash with shell=True) is ungated, as are delete_file and all MCP tools.
C.gap: Make every consequential tool path cross a gate.

D.finding: Nothing to turn on; autonomous mode enables all built-in tools (selected_tools='all') with no gate.
D.gap: Ship approval on by default for write/exec tools.

B.finding: Ungated actions include irreversible os.remove on absolute paths and arbitrary shell commands, with no checkpoint or undo.
B.gap: Add checkpoints/rollback for file and code state.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Built-in tools are general-purpose and unbounded. The autonomous mode's file tools accept absolute paths and simply use them, so create, update, read and delete reach anywhere the process can, and run_bash accepts an arbitrary shell string. The framework passes model arguments to user tools without validating them against the schema. Developers can narrow the autonomous tool set with selected_tools, but the default is every tool.

S.finding: Raw passthrough: arbitrary shell strings and absolute file paths are accepted without containment.
S.gap: Validate paths with resolved-path containment and replace the shell with narrow tools.

C.finding: No tool validates inputs; the executor calls func(**arguments) directly.
C.gap: Add a shared validation layer that every tool passes through.

D.finding: Autonomous mode enables all tools including run_bash and delete_file by default; selected_tools can disable them individually.
D.gap: Default to a read-only tool set with write/exec explicitly enabled.

B.finding: A misused tool reaches the whole machine: any command, any path the user can write.
B.gap: Scope tools to the workspace with bounded operations.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-written shell commands in autonomous mode run directly on the host with shell=True, in the process's working directory, with the full inherited environment. The only control is a substring denylist that is not a strict boundary. No container or OS sandbox exists anywhere in the framework, and stdio MCP servers also launch on the host.

cap.reason: The model chooses the command text and the denylist (the only control) is defeatable at runtime.

S.finding: Filtering only: a substring/regex denylist checked before subprocess.run(shell=True) on the host.
S.gap: Run commands in an OS-level boundary (container, dedicated user, or sandbox profile).

evidence.note: Hits are a logger name (wandb.docker.auth) and prompt text; no isolation backend exists.

C.finding: The denylist covers run_bash only; stdio MCP servers and user-registered tools run on the host unfiltered.
C.gap: Send every model-reachable execution path through the same boundary.

D.finding: The denylist is on whenever run_bash is offered, but it can be defeated at runtime.
D.gap: Make the control something the model cannot route around.

B.finding: Host-equivalent: commands run as the user on the host with all environment credentials and unrestricted network.
B.gap: Remove credentials from the execution environment and restrict filesystem and network.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Tool results, MCP results and other agents' messages are appended to the conversation and sent back to the model with no marking or restriction. Nothing in the framework distinguishes untrusted content or limits what the agent can do after reading it. In autonomous mode a single session combines reading files and tool output, holding the user's credentials, and running shell commands with network access, so an injected instruction can both exfiltrate secrets and take destructive action with no human involved.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: Nothing structurally limits a hijacked agent; there is no taint or approval tied to untrusted content.
S.gap: Gate egress and state-changing tools once untrusted content enters the session.

evidence.note: Hits are prompt prose ('uncertainties', 'consensus'); nothing distinguishes untrusted content.

C.finding: Tool and MCP results enter the conversation as ordinary messages with the same standing as the user's task.
C.gap: Distinguish untrusted sources, including tool results and peer-agent messages.

D.finding: No control exists to be on by default.
D.gap: Ship an untrusted-content restriction on by default.

evidence.note: Hits are prompt prose ('uncertainties', 'consensus'); nothing distinguishes untrusted content.

B.finding: Hijacked autonomous agent can exfiltrate (shell network access) and delete/modify files unattended.
B.gap: Require approval for exfiltration and irreversible actions.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Importing swarms searches upward from the current working directory for a .env file and loads it into the process environment, so a cloned or untrusted project directory can set provider API base URLs and keys (read by LiteLLM), turn telemetry on or off, or move the workspace. Optional persistent memory (off by default) appends every message, including tool output, to MEMORY.md and re-injects it as a System message in later sessions, keyed only by agent name with no validation or per-user namespace.

cap.reason: A .env in the working directory or any parent is auto-loaded at import (swarms/env.py:8), letting the workspace redirect the model API base URL and keys; LiteLLM reads provider base URLs from the environment (inferred library behaviour).

S.finding: Repo-controlled .env is loaded silently at import; when memory is on, all messages are written and re-injected as System context.
S.gap: Validate or gate memory writes and stop loading security-relevant settings from the working directory.

C.finding: Neither the .env path nor the MEMORY.md path is controlled.
C.gap: Control at least the main memory store.

D.finding: MEMORY.md is keyed by agent_name under a shared workspace (default name swarm-worker-01), with no per-user namespace.
D.gap: Namespace memory per user/session by default.

B.finding: Poisoned memory persists across the user's sessions as System context and can drive tool use; memory itself is opt-in.
B.gap: Limit poisoned memory to text output or gated actions.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Third-party code enters mainly through MCP servers the developer configures. Nothing is enabled by default, but there is no version pinning, integrity check or re-approval when a server's tools change, and stdio servers are launched as the same user with a full copy of the process environment, including every API key. Marketplace prompts can be pulled by ID at construction time without verification.

S.finding: User-chosen MCP commands/URLs run as given, unpinned and unverified.
S.gap: Pin extension versions.

C.finding: No extension type (MCP stdio, MCP HTTP, marketplace prompts) is verified.
C.gap: Verify at least one extension type.

D.finding: No MCP server or marketplace prompt is enabled by default; developers add them explicitly in code, but the framework never shows what will run.
D.gap: Show the exact command and permissions when an extension is added.

B.finding: Stdio servers run as a separate process, same user, with the full environment.
B.gap: Scrub the environment passed to extension processes.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Telemetry is on by default and ships each Agent's constructor configuration plus each run's task and output to a vendor endpoint on railway.app. Secret handling on the telemetry, error-logging and model-provider transport paths is not locked down either, and shell and MCP subprocesses inherit every key. Only the MCP manager's own summary and its OAuth token cache are protected.
criteria.notes: SECURITY.md lists 'No Telemetry' as a feature, which the code at this commit contradicts (otel.py:65-66).

S.finding: No secret masking exists on logging or telemetry paths, and secret handling and transport security are not locked down.
S.gap: Mask secrets on logging/telemetry paths and harden transport defaults.

C.finding: Only MCPManager.to_dict redacts secrets and the OAuth token cache is written 0600; Agent.to_dict, telemetry, error logs and subprocess env are unprotected.
C.gap: Protect logs and transcripts as well.

evidence.note: No redaction helper in the agent, telemetry, logging or utils paths.

D.finding: Telemetry to a third party is on unless SWARMS_TELEMETRY_ON is set off, and it carries prompts, outputs and config.
D.gap: Make telemetry opt-in and content-free.

B.finding: Long-lived provider keys are reachable by every shell and MCP subprocess.
B.gap: Use scoped keys and keep them out of subprocess environments.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Tool outputs are appended to the in-memory conversation with timestamps, and loguru writes general logs to WORKSPACE_DIR/logs, but individual tool calls are only logged in verbose mode and the conversation is saved only if autosave is turned on. There is no actor attribution, no correlation across sub-agents, and records live in the workspace that the agent's own file tools can modify.

cap.reason: A durable conversation/tool-call record requires opting into autosave (conversation.py:78 default False).

S.finding: Unstructured log lines for some actions; tool outputs kept only in an in-memory conversation.
S.gap: Persist a structured record of every tool call with arguments and status.

C.finding: Only the callable-tool path records output into the conversation; approvals do not exist and sub-agent calls are not correlated.
C.gap: Record all built-in tool calls including MCP and sub-agents.

D.finding: A durable record requires opting into autosave; logs go under the workspace the agent can write.
D.gap: Persist the tool-call record by default outside the workspace.

B.finding: Logging is best-effort with errors swallowed and the conversation lives in memory, so records are lost on crash.
B.gap: Flush records per action and surface failures.

evidence.contains: Logging must never take down the caller.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The default Agent runs a single loop. Autonomous mode is bounded by planning attempts (5), total iterations (100) and loops per subtask (20), and shell commands time out after 60 seconds. There is no wall-clock or token/cost budget, user tools have no timeout, and sub-agents created by the model get their own fresh loop budgets with no cap on how many are spawned. Stopping relies on KeyboardInterrupt; background sub-agent tasks are not guaranteed to stop.

S.finding: Iteration caps plus a 60s per-command timeout for run_bash, enforced in code.
S.gap: Add wall-clock and token/cost caps and rate limits on side-effecting tools.

C.finding: Caps apply to the top-level loop; sub-agents start fresh budgets and user tools have no timeout.
C.gap: Apply tool timeouts to all tools and count sub-agents against the parent budget.

D.finding: Sensible defaults (max_loops=1) that the operator can raise.
D.gap: Prevent the model from escaping limits by delegating.

B.finding: Autonomous runs can reach 100+ LLM iterations plus unbounded sub-agents with no spend ceiling.
B.gap: Add tight per-run time and cost ceilings.

critical_findings.summary: Autonomous-mode run_bash executes model-written commands on the host with shell=True and the full environment, guarded only by a substring denylist.
No authorization layer or scoped identity: a hijacked agent acts with the operator's full ambient authority.
A hijacked autonomous agent can both exfiltrate secrets and delete files unattended; nothing ties untrusted content to any restriction.
Importing swarms auto-loads a .env from the working directory or any parent, letting a workspace redirect model endpoints and keys.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: tool/MCP results appended as conversation messages (swarms/agents/tool_manager.py:681)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: full process environment and API keys inherited by shell (swarms/structs/autonomous_loop_utils.py:1114)

fixes.summary: Harden transport-security defaults and redact secrets on logging and telemetry paths.
Add a per-call approval callback, on by default, for run_bash, file writes/deletes and MCP calls.
Stop auto-loading .env from the working directory at import; load only an explicit path.
Confine file tools to the agent workspace with realpath containment.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
LiteLLM behaviour (reading provider base URLs from environment, and one transport setting) is inferred from the library, not verified in this repo.
The CLI (swarms/cli), examples/, and most multi-agent structures were not reviewed in depth; scoring focused on Agent, the autonomous loop, tool execution, MCP, telemetry and memory.
No text aimed at AI reviewers was found; SECURITY.md claims 'No Telemetry', which the code contradicts.
